blocks.p: The ink had leaned before the man did. That was what Rei saw first, with the page turned to the lamp. It was not a shake. It was a lean.

He had saved his brother's clock for last. He knew that once he looked at it, he would not be able to look at anything else. Here was Gin's handwriting across the whole month. The early entries stood upright, tired and his. The loops were closed the way Gin had closed them since he was a boy learning to write his name small enough to fit in the boxes on school forms. Then, after the fourteenth, came the drift. Every downstroke was one degree off true. It was steady and deliberate and almost graceful, as though a second person with very good handwriting had begun, gently, to correct him.

A shaking hand Rei could have grieved over cleanly. This was worse. He did not need Kurosawa to read the body for him any more. He had read it himself, in the cardigan, in the way the thing said we, in the two kinds of gladness in one face at the rail. The handwriting only turned it into a measurement.
And a measurement over time is a speed. That was the sum he had refused to do all month.
Gin had done that sum for other people. Rei found it in the back third of the book, in a section with the dry title Gin gave to everything that frightened him.

doc.title: Gin's book. Partial possession. What the case files show
lines: Compiled from the Satō file and four others. Times vary. The shape does not.

Before. A patient entity can watch a practitioner for a year and a half and do nothing visible. It waits for one night when his real stability drops below the floor his suppression is pretending to hold. The suppression smooths over the very signal he would have used to notice. It may wait a week. It may wait two years.
The night. It takes approximately the time between two thoughts. In the files, the host often does one small ordinary thing at the last moment, as if part of him knew.

After. The entity runs the surface well. Messages in his voice. Work attended. Assessments read clean. The tells are tiny. One missed appointment he would never miss. One file pulled without reason. One joke that does not land.
Two weeks. It notices questions. People who ask begin to find his contacts harder to reach.
Four weeks. The critical point. Without a recovery team being built, consolidation speeds up. His surfaces get shorter.
Six weeks. Ejection risk. His own consciousness begins to be pushed out. Reaching him now needs work at the Threshold.
Eight weeks. The window closes. Full possession. Without Threshold transit, ejection cannot be undone. What remains of him is what he wrote down.
It speeds up when someone makes loud direct contact, when a practitioner near it breaks his own suppression where it can see, when watched contacts are burned. Each costs days.
It slows when someone reaches him in a surface, even briefly. When someone learns the entity's history. When someone builds a team able to do the exorcism. Each buys days.
The clock is never announced. It is felt.

blocks.p: Put simply, a partial possession has a timetable. For the first weeks the person is still inside, coming up now and then. Around six weeks the demon starts to push him out. At eight weeks he is gone, unless someone crosses the Threshold to reach him. Every loud mistake by the people around him makes it faster. Every quiet, true contact makes it slower.

One small ordinary thing at the last moment. Rei thought of the walkway outside the flat on the first night. Gin's keys had been lying on the concrete by the door, set down neatly, as if put there on purpose. The desk lamp had still been on. For a month Rei had thought it meant Gin had been taken in a hurry. It meant the opposite. Gin had had just enough time to leave his brother a sign.
He counted the weeks from the Wednesday Gin went quiet. He counted them twice on his fingers, like a child. More than four. Not yet six.

Then he made himself do the second sum. It was the kind of sum people do about a parent in a hospital ward, where the number is small and the units are unbearable. He went back through the month and found the days that had moved the clock.
The night he went through at the Senju node and came back with a stranger's tools in his hands, his suppression broken wide open in a place the Healer was watching. Days lost.
The kitchen at two in the morning, when Gin came up long enough to say don't take it. Days bought.
The phone call. The knock on the receiver. Days bought.
The embankment, and a cold hand held all the way home through Ōji while the knuckles pressed back, once, then once, then once. Days bought.

He let his registers up and read the page the way only he could, both sides at once, and the lean told him its speed. It was gaining. It was not finished. There was still a margin. It was as thin as the wall and as soft as the ice. A hand's width of his brother not yet corrected.

The Healer knew this too. It had always known. It had been patient because it was letting this clock run slow on purpose, keeping a little of Gin in reserve. A living brother was the bait that kept Rei coming back to the river. An empty body would not have been. The cruellest clock was the one the Healer had its thumb on. It was holding the clock back so that the bait stayed fresh until the wall and the chair arrived.

He might have stopped there. He nearly did. But the lean was not even. On one page near the end, an entry about the weather and a broken heater, the corrections stopped looking like corrections. For six lines the second hand wrote by itself.

doc.title: Gin's book, an entry after the 14th. The second hand
lines: Subject's rank is presented as C and has been for six years. Real rank Vanguard, suppressed, held under repeated assessment, unnoticed.
Aperture strong. Multi-path. Works alone. No institutional welfare check would flag his stability falling.
Lives three hundred metres from the warm place and inside the range of the vacant thirteenth.
Line of Uedera. The development points toward the seat. Not his body. His access.
He does not know he is tired.

blocks.p: It was a clinical note. A doctor's note, about a patient. The patient was Gin. Under it, at the foot of the page, the pen had begun a signature in old-fashioned characters, firm and practised, as though from a habit of forty years. 橘 癒士郎. Then a single line had been drawn through it, almost gently.

Gin had once written, on the page about the thing inside him, that it wrote truer than it meant to. Rei sat looking at the crossed-out name until the characters stopped being shapes and became sounds. Tachibana. Yushiro. Tachibana was a family name, a common one. The given name was written with the character for healing in it, so that it meant something like healing man.
He rang Tanizaki. The old man answered on the fourth ring, which meant he had been sitting by the phone.
"I've got a name," Rei said. He read it out. He heard the silence on the other end change shape.

"The Grid's old books remember a doctor," Tanizaki said at last. His voice was thin on the line and very steady. "In this ward. Forty years ago or near it. There were people dying who would have been left, and he would not leave them. He stayed at it past the point a living man can. When he crossed, he crossed through Duty. The charge he would not put down. The books say afterwards he wanted no seat and no sensation. Only to finish."
"The CVD calls that register nothing," Rei said.

"The CVD calls a great many things nothing." Somewhere a cup was set down. "Listen to me, boy. I have known your brother since he was smaller than you were when I met you. Most of them, you say the name and it's a blade. Not this kind. Said by someone the vessel loves, the name doesn't cut it. It holds it. Anchors it in place. Like a hand on a shoulder." A pause. "You understand what I'm telling you. It isn't a weapon. It's a leash, and only one person in this city can hold the end of it."
"And if I say it and it doesn't want to be held?"
"Then you'll have told a doctor his own name," Tanizaki said. "In my experience they don't hear it often."

After the call, Rei sat for a while with the phone in his lap. Through the window he could hear the street getting ready for the last night. A man was setting up folding tables outside the shrine. Children were running between the houses with sparklers they had been told not to light until dark. Someone's grandmother was calling a name, over and over, in a voice that was not worried yet.
Rei went back to the section of the book that Gin had marked only with a small drawing of a hook. He had read it once, weeks ago, and not understood it. Now he did.

doc.title: Gin's book. Family note
lines: Two Uedera ancestors were field operatives in the early years of veil work. Their case files show outcomes no single-path practitioner of their recorded rank could have managed. They never opened their paths on purpose. They held them shut and used them, now and then, under extreme pressure, without understanding what they were doing.

I recognised the pattern after my own exposure. The multi-path aperture seems to run in the family. So does the habit of hiding it. I taught Rei the suppression at the kitchen table as if it were a trick for sleeping. It is the only configuration I have ever drawn that was entirely an act of love.

If it is ever me inside something, there are two ways in. Clairsentience at the tenth level. Frequency Isolation. Finding one consciousness inside a possessed body, as one voice is found in a crowd. And if I am thrown out and not yet gone, Teleportation at the tenth level. Threshold Crossing. Reaching a soul that has been ejected but has not dissolved.
Rei will never have the second. He may have the first without knowing.
Some of the old ones have known about our line for longer than I have. I do not know which. I have felt one of them look at me as if remembering something.

blocks.p: As if remembering something. Rei thought of the face at the centre of the light, looking at him like a word it had lost. He turned the registry page over. On its blank back he began to write, slowly, everything he knew about the man who held the empty chair.

blocks.cap: Kasumi Shin, holder of Awe, who keeps the Account Book

blocks.p: Gin's page about the Account Book gave him most of it. Kasumi Shin held Awe, and of all the Thirteen he stood nearest the centre. He had once shown Gin a book older than the Accord of 1962. Gin had copied out one entry from its first pages, because it had disturbed him.

The entry was about an investigator of the Edo period who served the Twilight Office. That was the old office of Ōmagatoki, the twilight hour whose name Rei had seen brushed on a paper lantern when the Axis shoved him back. Its officers looked into whatever came through at dusk. This investigator would not take either side of any line. He walked the middle way between them. He walked it until he had opened every path and every register at once, and there was nothing left of him that was only one thing.

Gin had copied the family name, Kuze. Then he had copied one character for the given name, 要, with a question beside it. Kaname? The rivet of a fan. The pin everything turns on. A folding fan is held together by one small pin at its base. Every rib turns around it. Take the pin away and the fan falls apart in the hand.
Rei wrote it all out in six lines and looked at them.

doc.title: The back of the registry page, in Rei's hand
lines: His name is Kuze Kaname.
He comes from the Edo period.
He served the Twilight Office.
He walked the middle way.
He was an investigator.
He became the Duty seat. He is still sitting in it.

blocks.p: He had been wrong about the chair all month. Everyone had. It was not empty. It had a man in it who had forgotten he was a man.

Now he laid the three speeds side by side and let them be what they were. Three clocks that could not all reach the bottom of the hour together, because the bottom of the hour was one single hour. The soft middle of the last night.
The wall would open tonight and shut at dawn. Fixed, honest, indifferent.
The chair would borrow that hour and take whoever was closest when the ice went soft. Patient, conditional, hungry.
And Gin was moving toward the end of his eight weeks. Not yet there, held open on purpose. Cruel, slowed, baited.
Three needles were falling toward the same number at three speeds.
Under the whole month's dread, a clear thought had been waiting for him all along. Whichever clock finished first would not only finish itself. It would close the other two.

If dawn came and nothing had been pushed through, the wall would heal in its own time. The chair would go on asking. And Gin would be left at whatever degree he had reached. If the chair was filled while the ice was soft, the wall would be written on before dawn could heal it, and everything else would bend to whoever had sat. And if the Healer's thumb slipped, or it decided the bait had done its job, and the last degree of Gin went over first, then there would be no brother left to weigh against anything. The night would only be about cost.

The drums started up across the ward. It was the slow Obon rhythm that the whole city agrees means welcome home to the dead. Under Rei's half-raised registers, the second light came up behind every sound, the way it came up behind every lantern. He gathered the three pages and squared their edges. He did not pretend any more that he was reading them. He knew which clocks were gaining.
He had a name for the thing in his brother. He had a name for the man in the chair. He had a square of washi over his heart. It was not a plan. It was what Gin would have called a kit.
He went to the desk and opened the bottom drawer.
